q: A bank wants to predict whether a new applicant will default within 12 months, yes or no. What kind of task is this?
options: Regression, because default risk is a score
Regression, because the bank holds numeric data on applicants
Clustering, because applicants form natural groups
Classification, because the outcome is a category
explain: Default or no default is a category, so this is classification. Regression predicts a continuous value such as a price or a time.

q: A fraud team has few investigators and wants most of its flagged cases to be real fraud. Which measure should it watch most closely?
options: Recall
Mean squared error
Precision
Accuracy
explain: Precision asks how many predicted positives are truly positive, so it matters when false positives are costly. Recall focuses on missed positives instead.

q: A hospital screening test must catch as many ill patients as possible, even at the cost of extra checks. Which measure matters most?
options: Precision
Accuracy
Specificity
Recall
explain: Recall is the share of actual positives that were caught, so it matters when missing a case is costly. Specificity concerns healthy people correctly cleared.

q: A model on a heavily imbalanced dataset always predicts the majority class. What will its accuracy look like?
options: High, even though it never finds a single positive case
Low, because it ignores half of the classes
Zero, because it never predicts the positive class for any record
Equal to its recall on the positive class
explain: Accuracy counts all correct predictions, and the majority class makes up most of them. This is why accuracy can mislead and measures such as F1 are preferred.

q: What does Gini impurity measure in a node of a decision tree?
options: How mixed the classes in the node are
How many features are left to split on
How deep the node sits in the tree
How many samples the node contains
explain: Gini impurity is the chance of mislabelling a random sample if it is labelled by the node's class mix. A pure node, where all samples share one class, has an impurity of zero.

q: Compare precision and recall and say when each matters most.
model: Precision asks, of the items predicted positive, how many are truly positive. It matters when false positives are costly, for example fraud investigations where staff time is limited. Recall asks, of all the real positives, how many were caught. It matters when missing a positive is costly, for example disease screening. The F1 score combines the two when a balance is needed.
points: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct
Recall is the share of actual positives that were found
Precision matters when false positives are costly with an example
Recall matters when false negatives are costly with an example

q: Explain how a decision tree decides which feature to split on.
model: A decision tree tries each possible split at a node and measures how pure the resulting child nodes are. Gini impurity shows how mixed the classes in a node are, and zero means all samples share one class. The tree calculates the weighted impurity of the children and compares it with the parent. The split with the largest drop, called the gain, is chosen. The same process then repeats on each child node.
points: Gini impurity measures how mixed a node is
Compares weighted child impurity with the parent to find the gain
Picks the split with the largest gain and repeats on the children

q: Explain how the K nearest neighbours classifier works. Discuss how the choice of K affects performance and generalisation. Explain why KNN is a lazy learning algorithm and a non-parametric model.
model: KNN is a supervised algorithm for classification. It classifies a new observation by measuring its distance to the training observations, often with Euclidean distance, and finding the K closest. The predicted class is usually the majority vote of those neighbours. A small K such as 1 makes the model sensitive to individual points and noise, which causes overfitting and high variance. A larger K gives smoother boundaries and less sensitivity to noise, but too large a K causes underfitting and high bias. K is usually chosen by cross-validation. KNN is lazy because it builds no explicit model during training and does most of its work at prediction time. It is non-parametric because it assumes no fixed functional form between the features and the classes.
points: Measures distance, for example Euclidean, to find the K nearest training points
Predicts by majority vote of the neighbours
Small K overfits and is sensitive to noise, large K underfits
Lazy because it builds no model in training and works at prediction time
Non-parametric because it assumes no fixed functional form
flag: The model answer follows the tutor's sample answer in the mock test.

q: Which is a characteristic of the K nearest neighbours algorithm?
options: It learns a fixed set of coefficients during training
It requires a predefined number of decision rules
It retains training observations for use during prediction
It constructs a decision tree from the training data
explain: KNN is lazy. It keeps the training data and compares each new point with it at prediction time.

q: What is a likely consequence of choosing a very small K in KNN classification?
options: Higher bias and lower variance
Greater sensitivity to noise in the training data
Reduced computational cost during prediction regardless of dataset size
The model becomes parametric
explain: With a very small K one noisy neighbour can decide the class, so the model overfits with high variance.
source: Tutor's mock test, multiple choice question 4
